title: Outliers II - The IQR Method
abstract:
The IQR method is the standard outlier rule for skewed data, and it is exactly
what a box plot draws. This document defines $Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the interquartile
range, derives the "minimum" and "maximum" fences
$Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ and $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$, explains where the constant
$1.5$ actually comes from (and what $3.0$ means), shows why the method is immune
to the masking that defeats the Z-score rule, and covers its own weakness:
symmetric fences on an asymmetric distribution.

blocks.t: The Rule
From the notes
Used when the data distribution is skewed.

where $Q_1$ is the 25th percentile and $Q_3$ is the 75th
percentile. Anything outside minimum or maximum is an outlier.
The definitions
\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1

The interquartile range is the width of the middle 50% of the data. It is a
measure of spread, exactly as the standard deviation is — but computed
from ranks rather than from squared deviations, which is what makes it robust.

blocks.cap:
The box plot is this rule. The box spans $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, the
 line inside is the median, the whiskers reach to the fences, and every point
 drawn beyond a whisker has been flagged by the formula above. When you look at
 a box plot you are looking at the IQR method.

blocks.t: The quotation marks around "minimum" and "maximum"

The notes write them in quotes for a reason: these are not the smallest and
largest values in the data. They are computed boundaries. In matplotlib the
whiskers are drawn to the most extreme data point still inside the fence,
which is why a whisker often stops short of the fence itself.
Why It Works Where the Z-Score Fails

blocks.cap:
Three distributions. On normal data the two rules broadly agree. On
 skewed data the $3\sigma$ boundary sits far out on the right and below the
 minimum on the left, while the IQR fences track the actual shape. On
 heavy-tailed data the Z-score rule flags almost nothing, because the outliers
 themselves have inflated $\sigma$.

blocks.t: The reason, in one line

$Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the median have a breakdown point of 25%; the mean and
standard deviation have a breakdown point of 0% (Topic 14). The IQR
fences are computed from the middle of the distribution, so the outliers do not
participate in setting the boundary that judges them.

blocks.cap:
Left: the false-positive rate as a function of the multiplier $k$,
 which is where $1.5$ comes from. Right: masking. As more extreme points are
 planted, the Z-score method detects progressively fewer of them; the IQR method
 detects all of them until they make up a quarter of the data.

blocks.t: Where 1.5 Comes From

The constant is not arbitrary. It was chosen by John Tukey, who invented the box
plot, to give a sensible false-positive rate on normally distributed data.
The derivation
For $X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$:

Q_1=\mu-0.6745\sigma,\qquad Q_3=\mu+0.6745\sigma,
 \qquad \text{IQR}=1.349\sigma .
(The number $0.6745$ is $\Phi^{-1}(0.75)$.) The upper fence is therefore

So on normal data the IQR rule is almost exactly a $2.7\sigma$ rule, and the
fraction it flags is
2\big(1-\Phi(2.698)\big) \approx 0.70% .
Use $k=3$ when you only want the extremes

$1.5$ is the default and flags roughly 0.7% of clean normal data. If you are
hunting genuine data errors rather than merely unusual values, $k=3$ is the
conventional stricter choice. Treat $k$ as a hyperparameter and tune it if the
downstream metric is sensitive.
Applying It: Trimming and Capping
Both strategies from Topic 28 use the same two numbers:

rows: Drop rows where $x <$ lower fence or $x >$ upper fence
np.clip(x, lower, upper) — every extreme value becomes the fence value

blocks.t: The same numbers appear in Topic 24

$Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ and $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$ are exactly the values used for
end-of-distribution imputation on skewed data. One pair of formulas serves
three purposes: drawing a box plot, flagging outliers, and imputing missing
values at the tail. Recognising that they are the same computation is worth more
than memorising three rules.
The Method's Own Weakness
Symmetric fences on an asymmetric distribution

The rule adds the same $1.5\,\text{IQR}$ to both sides. On a strongly
right-skewed column the right tail is genuinely long, so a symmetric fence flags
a large number of perfectly ordinary high values — while the lower fence may
fall below the data's minimum and flag nothing at all.
Two remedies:

items:
Transform first (Topic 18–19), then apply the rule to the
 roughly symmetric result. This is usually the right answer.

Use an adjusted box plot, which scales the fences by a robust
 skewness measure (the medcouple):
 $[\,Q_1-1.5e^{-4\text{MC}}\text{IQR},\;Q_3+1.5e^{3\text{MC}}\text{IQR}\,]$
 for $\text{MC}\ge0$. Available in statsmodels.

blocks.t: It is univariate

The IQR rule examines one column at a time. A point can be perfectly ordinary on
every individual column and still be a clear outlier in the joint distribution —
a person 150 cm tall weighing 120 kg is unremarkable on each column alone. For
multivariate outliers you need Mahalanobis distance, Isolation Forest or Local
Outlier Factor.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split, GridSearchCV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .55, 3000), [180., 205., 230., 12., 9.]]

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE RULE
# =====================================================================
q1, q3 = np.percentile(income, [25, 75])
iqr = q3 - q1
lower, upper = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr

print(f"Q1 (25th pct) {q1:7.2f}")
print(f"Q3 (75th pct) {q3:7.2f}")
print(f"IQR           {iqr:7.2f}")
print(f'"minimum" Q1-1.5*IQR = {lower:7.2f}')
print(f'"maximum" Q3+1.5*IQR = {upper:7.2f}')

outlier = (income < lower) | (income > upper)
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")
print(f"actual min {income.min():.2f}, max {income.max():.2f} "
      f"-- note these are NOT the fences")

# pandas, in three lines:
s = pd.Series(income)
Q1, Q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75])
mask = ~s.between(Q1 - 1.5*(Q3-Q1), Q3 + 1.5*(Q3-Q1))
print("pandas agrees:", bool((mask.values == outlier).all()))

# =====================================================================
# 2. WHERE 1.5 COMES FROM -- verified on normal data
# =====================================================================
z = rng.normal(0, 1, 500_000)
a, b = np.percentile(z, [25, 75])
print(f"\nQ1 {a:+.4f}  (theory {stats.norm.ppf(.25):+.4f})")
print(f"Q3 {b:+.4f}  (theory {stats.norm.ppf(.75):+.4f})")
print(f"IQR {b-a:.4f}  (theory 1.3490)")
print(f"upper fence {b+1.5*(b-a):.4f} sigma  (theory 2.698)")
print(f"flagged {np.mean((z<a-1.5*(b-a))|(z>b+1.5*(b-a))):.4%}  (theory 0.6977%)")

for k in [1.5, 3.0]:
    fence = 0.6745 + k*1.349
    print(f"k={k}: equivalent to {fence:.2f} sigma, "
          f"flags {2*(1-stats.norm.cdf(fence)):.6%} of normal data")

# =====================================================================
# 3. IQR vs Z-SCORE ACROSS DISTRIBUTIONS
# =====================================================================
def flags(v):
    m, sd = v.mean(), v.std()
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    return (np.mean((v < m-3*sd) | (v > m+3*sd)),
            np.mean((v < a-1.5*r) | (v > b+1.5*r)))

print(f"\n{'distribution':22s} {'z-score':>9s} {'IQR':>9s}")
for name, v in [("normal",          rng.normal(50, 10, 20_000)),
                ("right-skewed",    rng.lognormal(3.2, .7, 20_000)),
                ("heavy-tailed t3", rng.standard_t(3, 20_000)),
                ("uniform",         rng.uniform(0, 100, 20_000)),
                ("bimodal",         np.r_[rng.normal(20,4,10_000),
                                          rng.normal(70,4,10_000)])]:
    zf, qf = flags(v)
    print(f"{name:22s} {zf:9.2%} {qf:9.2%}")
# uniform: BOTH flag 0% -- there is no tail, so neither rule fires.
# bimodal: both flag ~0% -- the rules cannot see that there are TWO populations.

# =====================================================================
# 4. MASKING -- the IQR method is immune
# =====================================================================
base = rng.normal(50, 5, 300)
print(f"\n{'planted':>8s} {'z detects':>10s} {'IQR detects':>12s}")
for k in [0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 60, 120]:
    d = np.r_[base, [400.]*k] if k else base
    m, sd = d.mean(), d.std()
    a, b = np.percentile(d, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    zc = int(np.sum(np.abs(d-m) > 3*sd))
    qc = int(np.sum((d < a-1.5*r) | (d > b+1.5*r)))
    print(f"{k:8d} {zc:10d} {qc:12d}")
# The IQR method finds all of them until they reach ~25% of the data --
# its breakdown point. The z-score method collapses almost immediately.

# =====================================================================
# 5. TRIMMING vs CAPPING
# =====================================================================
trimmed = income[~outlier]
capped  = np.clip(income, lower, upper)
print(f"\ntrimming: {len(income)} -> {len(trimmed)} rows")
print(f"capping : {len(capped)} rows, {int((capped != income).sum())} values changed")
print(f"std   original {income.std():.2f}  trimmed {trimmed.std():.2f}  "
      f"capped {capped.std():.2f}")
print(f"skew  original {stats.skew(income):+.2f}  capped {stats.skew(capped):+.2f}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. THE WEAKNESS -- symmetric fences on an asymmetric column
# =====================================================================
skewed = rng.lognormal(3.5, 1.0, 10_000)
a, b = np.percentile(skewed, [25, 75]); r = b - a
lo, hi = a - 1.5*r, b + 1.5*r
print(f"\nstrongly skewed (skew {stats.skew(skewed):.1f}):")
print(f"  lower fence {lo:8.2f}  vs minimum {skewed.min():8.2f} "
      f"-> flags {np.mean(skewed<lo):.2%} on the left")
print(f"  upper fence {hi:8.2f}  vs maximum {skewed.max():8.2f} "
      f"-> flags {np.mean(skewed>hi):.2%} on the right")

# THE FIX: transform first, then apply the rule
lg = np.log(skewed)
a2, b2 = np.percentile(lg, [25, 75]); r2 = b2 - a2
print(f"  after log: skew {stats.skew(lg):+.2f}, "
      f"flags {np.mean((lg<a2-1.5*r2)|(lg>b2+1.5*r2)):.2%} -- balanced")

# =====================================================================
# 7. IT IS UNIVARIATE -- a multivariate outlier slips through
# =====================================================================
h = rng.normal(170, 8, 2000)                  # height cm
w = 0.9*(h-100) + rng.normal(0, 5, 2000)      # weight kg, correlated
h = np.r_[h, [150.]]; w = np.r_[w, [120.]]    # short AND heavy -> impossible pair

for name, v in [("height", h), ("weight", w)]:
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [25, 75]); r = b - a
    flagged = (v[-1] < a-1.5*r) or (v[-1] > b+1.5*r)
    print(f"\n{name}: last point {v[-1]:.0f}, fences "
          f"[{a-1.5*r:.0f}, {b+1.5*r:.0f}] -> flagged: {flagged}")
# Neither column flags it. But jointly it is absurd:
iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.001, random_state=0).fit(np.c_[h, w])
print("Isolation Forest flags it:", iso.predict([[150., 120.]])[0] == -1)

# =====================================================================
# 8. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER -- fences LEARNED from train
# =====================================================================
class IQRCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Cap at Q1 - k*IQR and Q3 + k*IQR, per column."""
    def __init__(self, k=1.5):
        self.k = k

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        q1, q3 = np.nanpercentile(X, [25, 75], axis=0)
        iqr = q3 - q1
        self.lower_, self.upper_ = q1 - self.k*iqr, q3 + self.k*iqr
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

n = 4000
X = np.c_[np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .6, n-20), rng.uniform(300, 900, 20)],
          rng.normal(35, 8, n)]
y = (0.02*np.clip(X[:, 0], 0, 120) + 0.05*X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 3.2).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

for name, steps in [
    ("none",       [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("IQR cap 1.5",[("cap", IQRCapper(1.5)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("IQR cap 3.0",[("cap", IQRCapper(3.0)), ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:12s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

# k is a hyperparameter -- tune it rather than assuming 1.5
gs = GridSearchCV(Pipeline([("cap", IQRCapper()), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
                            ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
                  {"cap__k": [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0]},
                  cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("best k:", gs.best_params_["cap__k"], round(gs.best_score_, 4))

capper = IQRCapper(1.5).fit(X_tr)
print("fences learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(2))
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and to production.
Worked Examples
IQR fences on a column
Step 1 – quartiles. Using linear interpolation (NumPy default):
Step 3 – fences.
\text{lower} = Q_1 - 1.5\cdot\text{IQR} = 13.75 - 5.25 = 8.5
\text{upper} = Q_3 + 1.5\cdot\text{IQR} = 17.25 + 5.25 = 22.5
Step 4 – classify. Every value lies in $[8.5,\,22.5]$ except $95$. The point 95 is an outlier.

Compare with z-score. The same column gives a z-score of about $2.64$ for $95$ (mean $=25$, population sd $\approx 26.5$), which is still inside $3\sigma$. The IQR method finds the point that the z-score misses, because quartiles are not affected by the outlier.
Summary
Everything on one page

items: The IQR method is used when the data distribution is skewed.

$Q_1$ is the 25th percentile, $Q_3$ the 75th
 percentile, and $\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1$.

"Minimum" $=Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$, "Maximum"
 $=Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$. Anything outside is an outlier.
 These are computed fences, not the actual smallest and largest values.
The box plot draws exactly this rule.

$Q_1$, $Q_3$ and the median have a 25% breakdown point, so
 outliers do not set the boundary that judges them — this is why the
 method does not suffer masking.

On normal data $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}=\mu+2.70\sigma$, flagging $0.70\%$.
 $k=3$ gives $\mu+4.72\sigma$ — Tukey's "far out" fence.

The same two numbers are used for end-of-distribution
 imputation on skewed data (Topic 24).

Weaknesses: the fences are symmetric even when the distribution
 is not (transform first), and the rule is univariate — it
 cannot see a point that is only extreme jointly.
The fences are learned parameters: fit on train only.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. IQR or Z-score — when do you use which?

Z-score when the column is approximately normal. IQR when it is skewed, heavy
tailed, or you do not want to assume a distribution. IQR is also immune to
masking, so it is the safer default; the Z-score rule is preferable only when
normality genuinely holds.
Q. Where does the 1.5 come from?

Tukey chose it so the fences sit at roughly $\mu\pm2.7\sigma$ on normal data,
flagging about 0.7%. The arithmetic: $Q_3=\mu+0.6745\sigma$ and
$\text{IQR}=1.349\sigma$, so $Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}=\mu+2.698\sigma$. The stricter
$k=3$ fence corresponds to $\mu\pm4.7\sigma$.
Q. Why doesn't the IQR method suffer masking?

Because the quartiles are computed from the middle of the distribution and have a
25% breakdown point. Adding extreme values barely moves $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, so the
fences stay put. The mean and standard deviation have a 0% breakdown point, so
outliers widen the very boundary meant to catch them.

Q. Your income column flags 8% of rows as outliers. Is something
wrong?

Probably not with the data — with the method. Income is strongly right-skewed,
and a symmetric fence flags a lot of genuinely ordinary high earners.
Log-transform first and re-apply, or use an adjusted box plot that scales the
fences by the skewness.

Q. A point is within the fences on every column. Can it still be an
outlier?

Yes. The rule is univariate. Someone 150 cm tall weighing 120 kg is
unremarkable on each column separately but implausible jointly. Multivariate
detection needs Mahalanobis distance, Isolation Forest or Local Outlier Factor.
Q. What does the IQR rule flag on uniformly distributed data?

Nothing. $Q_1-1.5\,\text{IQR}$ falls below the minimum and
$Q_3+1.5\,\text{IQR}$ above the maximum. That is correct behaviour — a uniform
distribution has no tail — and a useful reminder that the method describes
tails, not errors.
